newsitem.title: TANZANIA: U.N. Rwanda tribunal head defends his record.
newsitem.headline: U.N. Rwanda tribunal head defends his record.

text.p: The registrar of the U.N. Rwanda war crimes tribunal defended his performance on Saturday and said he would not resign despite a damning U.N. report alleging mismanagement and misconduct.

Andronico Adede, a Kenyan national, told a news conference in this northern Tanzanian town where the court is based that he and his colleagues had done much to get the tribunal working despite a critical lack of resources.

A report prepared by the U.N. inspector general, Karl Paschke of Germany, alleged abuses, administrative lapses and misconduct in the tribunal. The report has been presented to new secretary general Kofi Annan who promised on Thursday to make changes at the Arusha tribunal.
Adede said he had intention of resigning. "I see no reason to think of doing that. I am quite proud of what I am trying to do and I think I am succeeding," he said.

The tribunal was set up by the U.N. Security Council to prosecute genocide in Rwanda in 1994. It started its first trial on Thursday of a Rwandan Hutu former government official accused of genocide and crimes against humanity.

The first witness, a Rwandan Tutsi woman, testified in the court on Friday against Jean-Paul Akayesu, a former mayor in Rwanda's central Taba commune, where she said he ordered the killing of Tutsis and moderate Hutus.
She will continue to give her evidence on Monday.
Adede said he and his staff had worked extra hard to kick-start the court despite a lack of funds during the inception period, lack of offices and even cells for indicted suspects.
"The tribunal has been a success against all odds and is indeed fulfilling its mandate of bringing those accused of genocide to trial," Adede added.
He did not comment on Annan's pledge to take "decisive action" to make changes in the administrative apparatus of the tribunal.
A new acting chief of administration, Mohamed Said of Ethiopia, was sent to Arusha last month to replace George Anderson of Liberia who left in October.
U.N. officials say Mario Cianci, who holds Italian and U.S. nationality, will go to Arusha soon to temporarily take over personnel.

The Arusha controversy is fraught with racial overtones, with European employees complaining that the tribunal's administrators have given jobs to relatives and friends who have no qualifications and discriminated against non-Africans.
U.N. officials said they believed Africans would be replacing those expected to be released from their jobs.
They admitted privately that the problems were the result of a misperception of New York's responsibilities in the tribunal, which was to function as an independent entity.

Arusha was an unlikely venue for the tribunal, with primitive telephone and other communication links. The tribunal has indicted 21 people, seven of whom are held in Aurusha. Eight others are still at large and four are in detention in Cameroon. The United States and Switzerland hold one each.

Among four held in Cameroon is Colonel Theoneste Bagosora, described as giving military orders at the beginning of the 1994 massacres. His transfer has been delayed but tribunal officials said on Thursday an agreement had been signed with Cameroon for the transfer.
